playbooks.title: 📜 Playbook 1: The FAANG Promotion System (L4 ➜ L5 ➜ L6)
playbooks.subtitle: Synthesized rules from Steve Huynh (Ex-Amazon Principal) & Ethan Evans (Ex-Amazon VP)

rules.rule: 1. Hard Work Does Not Equal Growth
rules.insight: Doing 20% more tickets at your current level only proves you are a great L4/L5, not an L6. Delivery is the currency of trust, but scope expansion is the currency of promotion.
rules.action: Shift from 'How fast can I code this?' to 'What is the business impact and architectural risk of this feature?'

rules.rule: 2. Write Your Promo Doc 6 Months in Advance
rules.insight: Never wait for performance review season. Map out your accomplishments against the next level's leadership principles directly with your manager.
rules.action: Ask your manager: 'What specific gap separates my current output from L6 expectations today?'

rules.rule: 3. Focus on Systemic Alignment, Not Politics
rules.insight: Workplace politics is just human interaction. Make your work visible to skip-level leaders by delivering clear architectural RFCs and system metrics.
rules.action: Send bi-weekly 3-bullet execution updates to key project stakeholders.

playbooks.title: 💰 Playbook 2: Tech Salary Negotiation & $400k+ Counter-Offers
playbooks.subtitle: Synthesized rules from Steve Huynh & Negotiation Experts

rules.insight: Recruiters push hard for current TC or expectations. Deflect by asking for the target bandwidth for the position.
rules.action: Say: 'I'm focused on finding the right role fit. What is the approved compensation band for this level?'

rules.insight: Your market value is determined by competing demand. A single written offer from Meta or Google increases Amazon/Netflix leverage by 30-50%.
rules.action: Align interview schedules across 3-4 target companies to land offer letters in the same 14-day window.

rules.insight: Base salary caps out quickly due to internal pay bands. Equity grant vesting schedules and sign-on bonuses have far more flexibility.
rules.action: Request equity top-ups tied to performance milestones if base salary hits the cap.

playbooks.title: 🎯 Playbook 3: Mastering FAANG Behavioral & System Design Interviews
playbooks.subtitle: Synthesized rules from Live Mock Interviews with Meta/Amazon/Netflix Engineers

rules.insight: Candidate candidates get lost in code details during behavioral questions ('Tell me about a time...'). Start breadth-first with high-level outcome.
rules.action: Use the STAR method: 15 seconds Situation, 15s Task, 60s Action (your specific contribution), 30s Quantified Business Result.

rules.rule: 2. Frame Conflict Stories around Business Tradeoffs
rules.insight: Never make yourself the hero who defeated a 'foolish' coworker. Frame conflicts as conflicting technical constraints.
rules.action: Say: 'We had competing priorities between latency and data consistency, so we benchmarked both approaches.'

rules.insight: Senior candidates don't just solve the problem given; they clarify scale, edge cases, and failure modes before writing pseudo-code.
rules.action: Always ask: 'What are our SLA requirements, throughput limits, and data retention rules?'

videos.title: Negotiation Expert: How To 3X Your Tech Salary
videos.synopsis: High-yield tech career guidance from ex-Amazon Principal Engineer.
takeaways: Core premise: Your paid has nothing to do with your performance.

Final conclusion: Um so, definitely advocate for yourself.
videos.transcript: Your paid has nothing to do with your performance. They want the highest probability of a great outcome with the least time and effort. The types of questions that 90% of candidates fail on are super simple. >> This is Colin Lernout. He's one of the world's foremost experts in tech salary negotiation, and he's helped everyone from senior engineers to executives pulling seven figures get paid what they're actually worth. >> Wait, so you you cold emailed your CFO and you said, "I need more money." >> You know, fast forward a few years, I'm negotiating $600,000 a year more on a $2 million >> I asked him whether or not you need competing offers. >> It's a big myth that you need to have competing offers. Even at places like Google, you just have to push back on it. >> We covered how to know if you should stay at your current company or find a better offer. >> Do you really trust that your manager values you and knows how to get you to the next level? >> And then I asked him the question everyone wants the answer to. >> These AI offers are crazy. How do you get one of these offers? >> Yeah, it's funny. I There's a few different variations of this. >> Let's get into it. Today we're speaking with Colin Lernout. Colin is one of the world's foremost experts in tech salary negotiation. How did you get to be one of these experts in tech salary negotiation? I like what was the journey like to get there? >> Yeah, it's a good question. So, I actually didn't negotiate my first offer. When I first came to Silicon Valley, I was Canadian and I had a NAFTA visa that I was going for. So, it was at in 2016 when a certain presidential candidate was saying he's going to tear up NAFTA. And so, I was like, "I'm going to take the first offer they give me." But, immediately I started actually building a team internally when I got to Udacity and I saw that the least performing person on my team was actually making way more than the best person on my team. >> Like by how much? >> I would say probably 120k a year. And I just realized right then that like your paid has has nothing to do with your performance. >> Sorry, your the worst performer was getting paid the most. >> performer on my team was making like a hundred and twenty k more than the best performer on my team. What's going on here? So I started going deep into it and nerding out about compensation, negotiations. This is right before levels came out, right? So there wasn't a lot of info out there and then I did probably what would be a stupid move if I heard someone do this now. I cold emailed my CFO who I'd met maybe one time and I just said, I think I came in at the wrong level. I need this much equity. I was like, what did I do? I'm going to lose my job. >> Wait, so you you cold emailed your CFO? >> Yeah. >> And you said, I need more money. >> Essentially like I think I've been at the wrong level. I need this much equity based on what I'm seeing out there. >> How much did you ask him for? >> I asked him for a hundred thousand dollars a year more in equity. >> Like a cold like you didn't know this person. >> I didn't know him. Yeah, the CFO I'd met once maybe twice at like, you know, the get-togethers. >> What about that email made it so that email didn't backfire on you? Cuz I could imagine you like going out on a limb like that just being like, hey, I'd like a hundred thousand dollars more. I'm at the wrong level right now. Pay me. Like how did you do it in a way that actually got the result? >> Yeah, if I was advising myself back then, I would say absolutely don't do that. But it's also why a lot of people do take like bad negotiation advice is cuz like my friend did it. He just sent an email and he got a big increase or I did this last time and it worked for me. But you know, just because that worked for them once doesn't mean it's going to work each time and you might actually piss them off and you know, create a big problem. For me, I was just lucky enough that I had demonstrated enough value like versus my level. That CFO really kind of respected what we were doing in my group and the team. He probably talked to my VP and said, hey, should we do this? And my VP was like, yeah, definitely give him whatever he wants. VP was probably like he didn't negotiate coming in. That was probably a dumb idea. So I just got lucky on that one. But at the same time I realized that just asking a lot of people just don't do that. A lot of people just don't ask for whatever value they want. And if you don't ask, it's always going to be no. Now, you have to ask in a safe way. I wouldn't do it the same way I did it. But, at the same time, that was just like a big groundbreaker for me. And you know, fast forward a few years, I'm negotiating $600,000 a year more on a $2 million offer, right? So, those those lessons compound. And I just became a nerd. I started teaching every single one of my direct reports. I would be like, "This is how you negotiate for the next promo cycle." >> Like with me. >> With me. Negotiate with me so I can tell my VP why you should earn more money. You could ask my reports. Like they They're a bunch of them, especially ones who are like underrepresented. Because yeah, I just I just was totally baffled at when I came in why people who were performing really well were not being valued for it. >> Logically, I understand that if I don't ask for a raise, I'm not going to get it. It's always going to be no. How do I do it in a safe way? >> The biggest thing that I learned, I learned from when I was hiring people who were actually above my level. So, I just got into this position as I moved up pretty quickly at Udacity, where I was actually helping hire executives or people at my level. And it was in those meetings. And what I realized what they were doing is every single one of them wouldn't just negotiate an offer. They would get the first offer, and then they would go into due diligence mode. And they would say, "I want to talk to the hiring manager. I want to talk to the skip manager. I want to talk to the board member. I want to talk to XYZ person." They would do back channels on their managers. But, a byproduct of that, despite just like figuring out this is actually the right role for me, this is the right company for me, which is a great reason why anyone should do due diligence. The byproduct was that the hiring manager would then be like, "Oh, first I have a face-to-face touchpoint with this person right after the offer. So, I have this emotional connection. They're not just another candidate. They're asking me smart questions about the role, clarifying the role." But then I'm like, "Oh, and now I'm thinking about them not just like candidate XYZ, but the person who's going to give my career value, but also the business I'm trying to grow about value. And I'm excited to go to bat for them. And they would go and say like, "Oh, we're going to give you a title bump. We're going to give you more money here XYZ here. We're going to give you more equity." And they would just fight for them even without asking. And so, what I realized is that just like behind the scenes, there is a whole team of people outside just the recruiter who are involved in what your offer ends up being. And if you focus on the people, you're going to be able to do two things. Number one, you're going to know how much you can push. If those people aren't excited about you, you're going to know pretty easily and you don't push as hard. And number two, by having them behind the scenes, there's no misunderstanding. So, if you ask for too much, a recruiter might be like, "Oh, this guy is like BS-ing or, you know, we're never going to get this guy. He's not serious." Instead of let's just drop them or not increase their offer, the hiring manager is like, "Oh, actually no, he's really good. There must be some kind of misunderstanding. Let's actually give him something good or ask him a clarifying question." And so, you have that safety net behind the scenes. >> You said you nerded out on compensation, tech compensation. So, it sounds like you got an inside look into how executives, tech executives were negotiating for their own compensation. How else do you nerd out on compensation? >> Yeah, well, that was a couple years later that I got the executive view. But when I first started nerding out, I asked people There was one negotiation coach that I could find in all of Silicon Valley. And they weren't a negotiation coach. They were career coach who did a You got to see taught people around the world how to do like self-driving car engineering and AI engineering back in like 2016. So, they did a seminar for us on like how to negotiate. I was like, "Great. Like, I'm going to learn from this person." And I just asked people around me. I asked like my CEO. He gave me some great advice on how to work with executive recruiters, which was terrible advice for me at the time as a non-executive, but in the future helped me a lot. That's totally cool." They go and start the job and then like, "You actually have to move to headquarters now." And you're like, "Well, that wasn't what we had talked about." And there was this big hiring surge and so they just they dropped those people like a bad habit. >> Yeah, and that's when I talk to senior people who have this who don't have this ethical quandary anymore about like reneging, they cite exactly that. They say the business is always going to do what's in their best interest. If the situation changes, they're going to change their answer. So, why wouldn't I do that for me, right? Like they're not looking out for me obviously, so I'm going to look out for me. And so if they force me into this position, I'm going to take the bird in the hand, right? Not two in the bush. But if another opportunity comes up and they force me into this position, why wouldn't I look at that other opportunity? Just like if I was 6 months on the job and someone came with a great opportunity, why wouldn't I look at that one? >> Talk to me about negotiating things outside of dollars. Things like uh remote work, uh extra benefits like vacation time or other perks. How do you think about asking for those things during a negotiation? >> Yeah. Now, if a company is hardlined on work from home uh sorry, not work from home. Work in office. Five days a week, three days a week in office. The only times that we've been able to get people to go to like one day a week or fully remote is either they have a very good champion internally, the hiring manager just wants them and says there is no other candidate, or that candidate had such other good opportunities that and they were get taking like essentially like a cut to be able to go here or a big risk in trying to go here. So, it's kind of like the market of one candidates. I'm not saying you can't be a market of one candidate. I'm not saying it's one out of a thousand candidates. This is probably 20, 30% of candidates that are in this position but that just don't take advantage of it. So, all of the top AI companies force people to be in office like three to five days a week at least. But, we were able to get a candidate to have one day a week in office. And that was just because of their unique role in the company and their hiring manager, the recruiter said it's absolutely impossible throughout the entire process, absolutely impossible. Then, what happened? They talked to the hiring manager after they got the offer when they're trying to close them, the hiring manager was desperate to close this specific person, they said, "Sure, we're going to let you come in once a week." Other times though, you can kind of sneakily, unofficially get hybrid or remote work. We have a lot of people that say, "Hey, it's the policy, you have to come in three days a week or you're going to have to fly in once a week or or twice a month or something like that if you're in a different city." The under the table deal or like when they have the side conversation with the hiring manager it's like, "This will be for a little bit, but then we're going to slowly make that once a month and then like once a quarter, right?" And then it starts become something more sustainable for you. And if they don't fulfill on that promise if you have other opportunities you can then decide to move on, but then you get to take this chance as long as you're willing to take that upfront cost of going into office. So, those are the times where we've been able to negotiate it. Now, when you're with startups, just like much easier. Uh, lots of things are are less set in stone. Non-compensation things. Uh, big tech people going to startups for the first time. There are tons of things that they don't even know are negotiable or that they should even negotiate. How to value your equity, right? Like, you need to understand strike price and preferred price and all that. But one of the biggest things is when you leave, if you get a startup offer and they give you stock options, if you leave that company for about three quarters of startups now, it used to be 100% of startups, within 90 days, if you didn't put down all the money to exercise those options, which could be hundreds of thousands of dollars sometimes, for the options you vested, you put $100,000 down, there's no no promise that you're going to get paid out on that. That company might not be liquid. At a time when you're leaving the company and are unemployed, at a time when you're leaving the company, it might not be super bullish on the company. You have 90 days to put up the cash and decide that. So, I had a CPO at a company for 6 years, built them to be super successful, but had to put nearly a million dollars down for their exercise options. The company wouldn't extend their exercise window on the way out and wouldn't give them any financing, which is something companies can do to help people like that. Even this person that helped them grow this company so much. So, it's much easier to negotiate that on the way in and it's actually something that even seniors not even like director plus can can negotiate. And the simple way you do it is when you get to the offer stage, you agree on the big top level numbers, right? Total compensation, base, bonus, equity, etc. Say, "Cool, that all looks good." You get the employment agreement. The employment agreement will say it will refer to something called the equity plan. You tell them, "I want to look at the equity plan. I have some questions about specific terms that are standard terms." More standard now because 25% of companies have longer exercise windows, but that means three quarters don't. "How long will I have to exercise my options after I leave the company in an unforeseen circumstance?" You don't want to say you're quitting the company. You can ask for severance up front, especially if you're taking a big risk or joining something that is a big bet for that company, they don't know if it'll work out. And then you can ask for things like change in control if you're more of a director plus kind of candidate. Change in control means if the company gets acquired and you're not going to be part of the future of that company, you can accelerate the vesting of all your equity and actually get paid out a big amount then. And if you don't do that, you can miss out on tons and tons of value at that point. But, you just ask them the questions, "What are the standard terms?" We had a candidate who was a senior director at a series C company. They sent this to the company, just the questions. Usually, we wait for the reply, and then we reply with an ask. >> Mhm. >> They just sent saying, "Oh, it's actually 90 days, but we're going to give you a few years." >> Uh-huh. >> And 3 years, I think, is what they gave them. "Oh, change of control clause, we don't usually give it, but we're going to give you one." They just predicted that he was going to ask, so he didn't even have to ask and get it. But, usually we just send a second email saying like, "These are the standard terms I expect based on companies now. I want to be able to bet on the future of the company, so if you can give me this, that'd be great." >> This is awesome. This is like, how is anybody supposed to know the questions to ask to unlock all of this value? >> The startup stuff? I worked with hundreds and even thousands of startup employees. I would say probably 10% of them know like half of the things >> Yeah. >> that I've learned by doing this stuff. Like, they just don't even know what's possible. Executives in these companies, sometimes we have to tell the company There was a $10 billion consumer AI startup where we spent 2 weeks in email with their team explaining how all these equity terms work to them. Even telling them like, "You should have this for the rest of your executive team. You just Your executive team just didn't know they could ask for it." And so, that happens actually sometimes. We'll tell them like, "Not just for me, like all of you guys should have this." And they're like, "Okay, great. Let's give it to everybody." Yeah, definitely important because you can be in a pretty tight pinch if you don't think about the downside. The way I think about it, it's much easier to negotiate the pre-nup than it is to negotiate the divorce. So, negotiate those things up front. >> Colin, uh thanks so much for having this conversation today. I learned so much about negotiation. If they wanted to work with you on salary negotiations, like uh how could somebody do that? >> Yeah, that's a good question. So, go to feelvalued.co. You'll either work with myself directly or my team of ex-Fanger executive recruiters. You get a free call. We'll help you out, like give you some strategies, and we'll tell you about the service if you want to work with us. There's no pressure, but you can decide to work with us. We work on a performance-based basis and yeah, we worked with everyone from seniors all the way up to like we said the like five, seven million dollar folks. Even if you're mid-career right now, uh it's always good to have someone in your corner. To be honest, like if you take away anything from this, whether you go with us or whether you do it yourself, try to negotiate. Even if you get a small increase, 10K, 20K, whatever it is, that might not seem meaningful. What I found in the data is that as your career goes higher, the people who make more not only earn a higher uh increase in their offers from first to last offer in dollar amount, but in percentage. So, you might only be able to get a 10% increase when you're early in your career, but when you're making 5, 600,000, you can get like 30, 40% increases sometimes. So, the broad the range grows and so everything you learn now, even if it doesn't work out in your specific case, will compound and you're going to be able to get those big increases later in your career. So, definitely it's something I'd invest in as a skill through that's going to be helpful in your company, between jobs, whatever it is. Even just like vying for your project and your teammates. Um so, definitely advocate for yourself. >> Thanks so much. >> Yeah. >> Thanks, Steve.
